extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Idler; aspiring painters, artists, and an educated 18th-century public
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for choosing and composing subjects for painting—especially historical or narrative pictures—and for understanding the distinct aims of portrait painting. Includes principles about what sorts of actions and moments are paintable and what makes a picture instructive and affecting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of subject for painting (instantaneous vs successive)
rubrics_metrics.description: He must have an action not successive but instantaneous; for the time of a picture is a single moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A painter should choose events that can be represented in one moment; subjects composed of several distinct actions that occur at different times (example: the death of Hercules as imagined with multiple incidents) do not unite into a single pictorial moment and therefore make poor subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must be circumstantial and distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: The action must be circumstantial and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the salient features of an event cannot be embodied in particular attitudes or a single clear action, the scene will not read as a picture. Example: a moving supplication in Homer cannot be effectively painted because language, not posture, supplies its force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject should excite varied passions among actors
rubrics_metrics.description: The event painted must be such as excites passion, and different passions in the several actors, or a tumult of contending passions in the chief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose moments that allow contrast and interplay of emotions (fear, joy, grief, pride) across figures so the picture can convey dramatic tension. Examples suggested: discovery of Ulysses by his nurse (mixture of surprise and guarded emotion) and the death of Epaminondas (mixture of gladness, grief, composure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositional variety — number and disposition of figures
rubrics_metrics.description: A picture with only two figures will want variety; a nobler assemblage furnishes more variety and expressive range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subjects that permit a range of faces and attitudes to display different passions and social relations; consider assemblies where multiple roles and reactions provide visual interest and instructional force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrait painting's social and affective purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrait painting is employed in diffusing friendship, in reviving tenderness, in quickening the affections of the absent, and continuing the presence of the dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portraits should aim to preserve and communicate individual presence and affective ties rather than merely ostentatious splendour; their value lies in social/affective function as much as in likeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius and national patronage for historical painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is chiefly exerted in historical pictures; patronage is due to encourage that art and to give beginning to a national school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical painting is the highest exertion of talent and needs institutional reward and patronage to flourish; offering prizes or commissions for historical subjects will foster ambitious work and an English school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects that yield instruction and moral exemplarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The event should provide 'irresistible instruction' and 'unexampled variety' through contrasted passions and moral situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select historical moments that can be composed to instruct (e.g., the dissolution of the parliament by Cromwell) where the contrast of characters and moral consequences can be clearly depicted and read by viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of painting to represent language-dependent sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Some scenes rely upon language and cannot be painted, because no peculiarity of attitude can supply the place of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choosing incidents whose emotional force depends chiefly on spoken words or narrative explanation; if the sentiment cannot be embodied in visible attitudes or expressions, the painting will fail to communicate the intended effect (example: certain Homeric supplications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory as the source-material for imagination and narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory is the primary and fundamental power; its two offices are collection and distribution: collection in youth and distribution in age; imagination recombines ideas from memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In literary or pictorial composition, use the stores of remembered images (collected in youth) as raw material for imaginative recombination; be aware that recollection often mixes pleasure with pain, and revived ideas in narrative will commonly carry associative sadness as well as delight—a composer should use this to deepen emotional texture.
